title: Microservices Quick Revision
summary: Night-before revision notes on monolith vs microservices: service boundaries, discovery, sync vs async calls, timeouts, service mesh, database per service, strangler fig migration, and when to avoid microservices.

chapters.title: Monolith vs Microservices: The Mental Model
points: Monolith = one deployable unit, one codebase, one database; calls between modules are in-process function calls (fast, transactional).
Microservices = many small independently deployable services, each owning one business capability and its own data, talking over the network.
Core trade: microservices swap code complexity for distributed-systems complexity (network failures, latency, partial failure, eventual consistency).

Comparison rows: deploy (all-or-nothing vs per service), scaling (whole app vs per service), tech stack (one vs polyglot), debugging (one stack trace vs distributed tracing), transactions (ACID vs sagas).
Modular monolith = one deployable with strict module boundaries; the usual best starting point and a cheap path to split later.

chapters.title: Service Boundaries and Database per Service
points: Draw boundaries around business capabilities / DDD bounded contexts (Orders, Payments, Inventory), not technical layers (UI, DB, logic).
Good boundary test: a typical change touches one service, and the service can deploy without coordinating with others.
Database per service: each service owns its schema; no other service reads its tables, only its API or events.
Cross-service consistency uses sagas (local transactions plus compensating actions) and eventual consistency, not distributed 2PC; reporting uses events or a read model, not cross-service joins.
Shared database or distributed monolith (services that must deploy together, chatty calls) is the classic boundary mistake.

chapters.title: Service Discovery and Sync vs Async Calls
points: Service discovery: instances come and go with autoscaling, so callers look up healthy addresses by service name via a registry (Consul, Eureka) or platform DNS (Kubernetes Service name).
Client-side discovery: the caller queries the registry and load-balances itself; server-side: a load balancer or proxy resolves it for the caller.
Synchronous (HTTP/REST, gRPC): caller waits for the reply; simple and immediate, but couples availability and latency, so the chain's availability is the product of each service's availability.

Asynchronous (queue or event broker like Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS): caller publishes and moves on; decouples services and absorbs spikes, but adds eventual consistency, duplicate delivery (make consumers idempotent) and harder debugging.
Rule of thumb: sync for queries needing an immediate answer, async for commands and events that trigger follow-up work.

chapters.title: Timeouts and Resilience
points: Always set a timeout on every remote call; the default is often infinite or very long, and one slow dependency exhausts threads and cascades into an outage.
Set the timeout from the dependency's observed p99 latency, and keep caller timeout greater than callee timeout, with the total fitting inside the user-facing deadline.
Retry only idempotent calls, with exponential backoff plus jitter and a capped retry count; unbounded retries cause retry storms.
Circuit breaker: after N failures it opens and fails fast, then half-open lets a probe through to test recovery.
Bulkhead (separate thread or connection pools per dependency) isolates failures; always define a fallback such as cached data or a degraded response.

chapters.title: Service Mesh and Sidecars
points: Service mesh moves networking concerns (mTLS, retries, timeouts, load balancing, metrics, tracing) out of app code into the infrastructure layer.
Sidecar pattern: a proxy container (Envoy) runs beside every service instance and intercepts all its inbound and outbound traffic.
Data plane = the sidecar proxies that carry traffic; control plane (Istio, Linkerd) pushes config, policy and certificates to them.
Gives you uniform mTLS, traffic splitting for canary releases, and observability across languages without code changes.
Costs: extra latency hop, CPU and memory per pod, and operational complexity; skip it for a handful of services, or consider sidecarless (ambient) mode.

chapters.title: Strangler Fig Migration, When Not to Use, and Cheat Sheet
points: Strangler fig: put a facade (API gateway or proxy) in front of the monolith, then extract one capability at a time to a new service and reroute that path, until the monolith is empty and retired.
Migration order: pick a low-risk, loosely coupled capability first, run old and new in parallel, shift traffic gradually, then delete the old code; never do a big-bang rewrite.
Don't use microservices for: small teams, early-stage products with unclear domain, simple CRUD apps, or without CI/CD, monitoring and tracing maturity.
Microservices pay off when: many teams need independent deploys, parts have very different scaling needs, and domain boundaries are stable.

Cheat sheet: boundaries by business capability; one DB per service; timeout on every call; retry only idempotent with backoff and jitter; sync for queries, async for events; mesh only at scale; start modular monolith; strangle, never rewrite.
